extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, marketers, businesses and individuals submitting news or press releases to WebWire (and similar wire services)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing and formatting news and press releases intended for online distribution and media pickup, emphasizing journalistic tone, structure, content, and submission metadata. Focused on releases distributed via WebWire and similar services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish News Releases vs Press Releases
rubrics_metrics.description: News Releases as distribution of properly formatted articles primarily to online news readers, generally bypassing the media. Press Releases as distribution that primarily delivers your news to targeted media (reporters, registered media and trade publications) and media-only wire services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate type depending on whether your goal is driving website traffic to readers (news release) or getting media attention/coverage (press release). Note: media-targeted distribution affords higher credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a Reporter, Not an Advertiser (Third Person Writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: News and Press Releases purport to report on an event, circumstance or occurrence by an independent reporter (a third person). When writing a news or press release, be that reporter and bring your content to the attention of readers as if you had no marketing agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in third person; avoid first-person phrasing such as 'I, John Doe...'; phrase information as reporting ('According to John Doe, ...'). Present facts, avoid promotional language and overt marketing tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Advertising Signals (tone and punctuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation marks ('!') conveys that your release is advertising, not news, and it’s the credibility of news that generates the good publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use exclamation marks; avoid copy that reads like an ad. Ensure the tone reads journalistic and credible rather than promotional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and Paragraph Count
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases are most effective when they are under 500 words, generally two to three paragraphs, preceded by a clear and attention-grabbing headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for brevity: keep the whole release under 500 words and structured in roughly two to three paragraphs for effectiveness, while the body should be more than one paragraph with a final summary paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Be creative and keep it to one sentence. Capitalize the first letter of all words but do not use all upper case letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use title case (capitalize the first letter of each word), keep to one sentence, and avoid ALL CAPS. Make the headline attention-grabbing but not sensational. Avoid exclamation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Paragraph: Lead with Location/Date and the Five W's
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical location (country, state, city) (month, date and year) - Begin with a strong introductory paragraph that captures the reader’s attention and contains the information most relevant to your message such as the 'Five W's' of (W)ho, (W)hat, (W)hen, (W)here, and (W)hy, when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the lead so that if it were the only paragraph read it would convey the entire message; include a hook to encourage further reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Inverted Pyramid Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective releases usually utilize a strategy known as the inverted pyramid, which is written with the most important information and quotes first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the most newsworthy facts and strongest quotes early; follow with supporting detail and background toward the end so editors can trim from the bottom if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body Content: Detail, Quotes, and Grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: These paragraphs should contain more detailed important information, and make up the body of the release. Pick up with the information provided in your first paragraph, including quotes from key staff, customers or subject matter experts. Make sure you use correct grammar so as not to affect your credibility negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include relevant quotes from authorized persons, expand on the lead's facts, and maintain high grammatical standards. Ensure quotes and factual claims are cleared and attributable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle and Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very important to maintain factual accuracy, make sure you are cleared to use quotes or information about businesses, and most importantly have an angle that will appeal to readers and journalists (often by connecting your release to current events or issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft an angle that makes the release relevant to media and readers—tie to trends, events, or broader issues. Avoid boilerplate that lacks news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Paragraph: Restate and Summarize Key Points
rubrics_metrics.description: The final paragraph should restate and summarize the key points of your release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the closing paragraph to reinforce the main message and provide a tidy conclusion or call-to-action reference for reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide Additional Information and Links
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide avenues for the reader to obtain additional information, demos, samples, etc., and it is important to include Internet links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include URLs for more information, downloadable assets, product demos, or sample materials. WebWire provides submission fields for company name, contact, telephone, email, website, and other online connections—use them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Links Must Lead to Information, Not Advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Also, all inclusive links must lead to information, not advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure any links included point to factual, informational pages (e.g., press kit, product specs, background), not purely promotional landing pages or ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact Information Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: With a WebWire submission, include contact information about the release (name, title, email, telephone, etc.) within the appropriate online form. Make sure it is the person who can answer questions about the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide complete and accurate contact details and use a contact who is available and authorized to answer media inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Legal/Background Details and Disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Include trademark acknowledgments, product or event timelines, availability, logistics, etc. in paragraph form and also provide background information about the persons or organizations featured in the release, as well as any applicable disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add necessary legal acknowledgments and practical details (timelines, availability) and concise background or boilerplate about the organization to aid reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and Credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember, this content may be used by the media in their reporting, so be accurate and reasonably detailed and make sure your contact data is accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize factual precision and verifiable claims; inaccuracies will damage credibility and reduce chances of media usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission Metadata and Use of WebWire Fields
rubrics_metrics.description: WebWire provides special data submission fields for company/agency name, contact, telephone, email address, website location, etc. and other online connections (links).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate all provided metadata fields in the submission platform (company name, contact info, website) rather than burying this information only in the body text.
